name: Git in a Team
author: Recurse
subject: swe
description: Work like a teammate: feature branches, pull requests, code review, merge vs rebase vs squash, conflicts, CI and releases.

lesson.intro: `git add` and `git commit` get you through a solo project. A team adds pull requests, reviews, protected branches, CI and releases, plus the etiquette that keeps it friendly. This is the workflow from your first ticket to your first release.
objectives: Take a ticket from a fresh feature branch to a merged pull request
Write commit messages and PR descriptions reviewers thank you for
Give and receive code review that is useful and kind
Choose merge, squash or rebase, and resolve conflicts in either flow
Use .gitignore, branch protection, SemVer and tags like real teams

sections.title: Feature branches and the pull request flow
sections.key: Never commit straight to `main`: branch from a fresh main, push with `-u`, open a pull request, and merge once it is reviewed and green.
sections.body:
Your first ticket, PROJ-142, adds a CSV export button. `main` is the shared, always-deployable line, usually protected, so you work on a **feature branch** and propose the change in a **pull request** (PR; GitLab calls it a merge request).

[[visual]]

[[code]]

**Keep branches short-lived**, ideally a few days: the longer a branch lives, the further main drifts and the bigger the final merge. Ship big features in slices, hiding unfinished parts behind a feature flag.

Open a **draft** PR early to run CI and invite feedback without risk of an accidental merge.

steps.label: Switch to main and pull
steps.detail: Start from the latest code with a clean working tree

steps.label: `git switch -c feature/csv-export`
steps.detail: Many teams add the ticket: proj-142-csv-export

steps.label: Push with `-u` and open a PR into main
steps.detail: CI runs the checks; teammates review the diff

steps.label: Push fixes to the same branch
Approved and green: merge, delete the branch

sections.code:
git switch main
git pull                  # latest main
git switch -c feature/csv-export

# ...edit, run the tests...
git add reports/ tests/
git commit -m "Add CSV export for reports"

# first push: create and track the branch
git push -u origin feature/csv-export

# after review comments, on the same branch:
git commit -am "Escape commas in cells"
git push
sections.deeper:
Teams that take short branches furthest merge small changes into main at least daily and call it **trunk-based development**. You may also hear of Git Flow, with long-lived `develop` and `release` branches; it still exists, but most web teams have moved to the simpler short-branch model described here.

On a protected main, a direct `git push origin main` is rejected by the server anyway, which is one more reason the PR is the only road in.
sections.tip: Before starting any new branch, run `git status` and make sure you are on an up-to-date `main` with a clean working tree.
sections.pitfall: Starting a new branch from wherever you happen to be, such as another unfinished feature branch. Your PR then drags in its commits too. Switch to main and pull first.

activity.title: Branch like a teammate
activity.prompt: Work through the scenario steps. Each time you commit, watch which branch label moves along with HEAD and which stays where it was. That is all a branch is: a movable label on a commit, which is why creating one is instant and cheap.

check.question: You run `git push` on a brand-new local branch and git complains that it has no upstream branch. What do you run?
choices: git pull origin main
git push --force
git push -u origin feature/csv-export
git branch --delete feature/csv-export
check.explanation: -u (--set-upstream) creates the branch on origin and records it as the upstream, so later git push and git pull know where to go. Force-pushing or pulling main does not create the remote branch.

sections.title: Commit messages and PR descriptions
sections.key: A commit subject is a short imperative summary and its body explains why; a pull request stays small and says what, why and how to test.
sections.body:
Six months from now someone runs `git blame` on a confusing line and reads your message. Compare `fix stuff` with `Fix double charge when the payment webhook is retried`.

[[visual]]

[[code]]

**Conventional Commits** add a prefix that tools parse for changelogs and versions: `feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, `refactor:`, `test:`, `chore:`. `feat!:` or a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer marks a breaking change. Follow what your repository already does.

[[visual 2]]

**Keep PRs small.** 150 lines get a careful review within hours; 2,000 lines get a skimmed "LGTM" or wait a week. Split big work: a refactor PR first, then the feature.

visual.title: Commit message rules
rows: Subject of about 50 characters, imperative ("Add", "Fix"), no trailing period
It completes "If applied, this commit will..."
A blank line, then a body wrapped at about 72
The body explains **why**; the diff already shows what
Easy to review, and to revert cleanly

visual.title: A PR description covers
rows: A sentence or two and the ticket. `Closes #123` closes that issue when the PR merges
The approach, and alternatives you rejected
Steps or commands a reviewer can run
Screenshots for UI changes; risks, migrations, follow-ups

sections.code:
$ git log -1 --format=%B
Fix double charge on webhook retries

The payment provider retries a webhook
when our response is slow. The handler
charged the order on every retry. Store
each event id and skip events we have
already processed.

Closes #482
sections.pitfall: Messages like `wip`, `fix` or `changes`. If your team squash-merges, the PR title becomes the commit message on main, so write the title just as carefully.

check.question: Which is the best commit subject line?
choices: Fixed the bug
Prevent duplicate orders when Pay is double-clicked
WIP: orders, payments and some cleanup
orders.py updated
check.explanation: It is imperative, specific and short, and says what the commit does for users. The others are vague, describe the file rather than the change, or mix several changes in one commit.

sections.title: Code review etiquette: giving and receiving
sections.key: Review the code, not the person: ask questions, explain why, label how much each comment matters, and reply to every comment you receive.
sections.body:
Code review shares knowledge, catches bugs and keeps the codebase consistent. Done carelessly, it also hurts feelings.

[[visual]]

Label comments so the author knows what matters: `nit:` (tiny, optional), `question:`, `suggestion:`, `blocking:` (must change before merge). Style preferences then cannot hold up a PR, and real problems are not ignored.

[[visual 2]]

A review ends with **Comment**, **Approve** or **Request changes**. Many repositories require an approval, sometimes from a **code owner** listed in `CODEOWNERS` for that folder.

items.title: Giving a review
points: Read the description and ticket before the diff
Focus on correctness, edge cases, tests and security; leave formatting to linters
Ask rather than command; explain why and offer an alternative

items.title: Receiving one
points: Review your own diff first: leftover prints, commented-out code
Reply to every comment: fix it, or explain why not
Push fixes as new commits, not rewritten history, so reviewers see what changed
Move a long thread to a call, then record the outcome

visual.title: Same point, kinder
rows: "If rows is empty, rows[0] raises IndexError. Could we return an empty CSV early?"
"Why would you do it like this?"
"question: is there a reason to load every order into memory? A generator might be safer."
"nit: d -> due_date would make line 40 easier to read. Not blocking."

sections.deeper:
GitHub's suggestion blocks let a reviewer propose an exact edit that the author accepts with one click, which turns many comments into a few seconds of work.

Rewriting your branch with an interactive rebase in the middle of a review replaces the commits the reviewer already saw, so they can no longer see just what changed since their last pass. Tidy history before requesting review, or after approval if your team squashes anyway.
sections.pitfall: Bikeshedding: twenty comments about names and spacing and none about the missing error handling. Spend attention on what can break, and let tools enforce style.

check.question: A variable name could be clearer, but it does not affect correctness. What is the best review comment?
choices: "Rename this."
Request changes and block the merge until it is renamed
Say nothing, because naming is personal taste
"nit: cnt -> retry_count would read more clearly. Not blocking."
check.explanation: The nit label tells the author it is optional, and the concrete suggestion with a reason makes it easy to act on. Blocking a merge over a name wastes everyone's time, and staying silent loses an easy readability win.

sections.title: Merge, squash or rebase
sections.key: Merge commits keep everything, squash makes one commit per PR, rebase makes a straight line; rebased commits are new, so never rebase commits others built on.
sections.body:
Your PR is approved. The merge button offers three options, each leaving different history on main:

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

Many teams squash most PRs; consistency is what matters. After a squash, git does not see your branch as merged, so delete it and start the next task from main.

Locally, `git rebase main` replays your commits on top of main. They get **new hashes**, because a hash covers its parent. Golden rule: **never rebase commits others have based work on**, such as main.

Rebasing your own pushed branch is normal: update it with `git push --force-with-lease`, which refuses if someone pushed since your last fetch. Before review, `git rebase -i main` lets you squash, reorder, reword or drop your commits.

items.title: Create a merge commit
points: Adds a merge commit with two parents
Exact record, but main becomes a braid

items.title: Squash and merge
points: One new commit holding the whole PR

items.title: Rebase and merge
points: Best when every commit is clean

visual.title: main afterwards
visual.caption: Starting from main A, B, C and a feature branch D, E that split off at B. M has two parents (C and E); S holds the changes of D and E; D' and E' are new copies with new hashes.

sections.deeper: Why the golden rule matters: if you rewrite main and force-push it, every teammate is left holding commits that no longer exist upstream, and their next pull tangles the two histories. Plain `--force` overwrites blindly; `--force-with-lease` checks that the remote is where you last saw it.
sections.pitfall: Force-pushing with plain `--force` after a rebase. If a teammate pushed a fix to your branch meanwhile, it is silently gone. Use `--force-with-lease`.

activity.title: Replay commits with rebase
activity.prompt: Follow the scenario steps, and look closely at the graph before and after the rebase. Your commits end up on top of main as a straight line, and their hashes change, because rebase creates new commits rather than moving the old ones.

check.question: After `git rebase main`, why do your branch's commits have different hashes?
choices: Rebase replays them as new commits on a new parent, and the hash covers the parent
Git renumbers every commit in the repository after a rebase
The hashes only look different until you push
Rebase compresses the commits, which changes their content
check.explanation: A commit's hash is computed from its content, metadata and parent. Rebase gives each commit a new parent, so each one becomes a new commit with a new hash. That is why rebasing shared commits causes trouble.

sections.title: Staying up to date and resolving conflicts
sections.key: Bring your branch up to date by rebasing onto or merging `origin/main`; in a rebase conflict the HEAD side is main and the bottom side is your commit.
sections.body:
While your PR was in review, three other PRs landed. If one changed your lines, you get a **conflict**: two people changed the same lines, so a human decides.

`git fetch origin` downloads the new commits without touching your files. Then follow your team's convention:

[[visual]]

[[code]]

In a merge, `HEAD` is your branch. **In a rebase the sides flip**: rebase stands on main and re-applies your commits, so `HEAD` is main (plus commits already replayed) and the bottom part is your commit.

[[visual 2]]

`git merge --abort` or `git rebase --abort` puts everything back as it was before you started.

items.title: `git merge origin/main`
points: Adds a merge commit to your branch

steps.label: Edit each to the right final code
steps.detail: Often combining both changes, not picking a side

steps.label: Run the tests
steps.detail: A file without markers can still be broken

steps.label: `git rebase --continue`
steps.detail: or `git commit` to finish a merge

sections.code:
$ git fetch origin
$ git rebase origin/main
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in config.py
error: could not apply d2a69bf... Raise upload timeout

$ cat config.py
<<<<<<< HEAD
TIMEOUT = 45
=======
TIMEOUT = 60
>>>>>>> d2a69bf (Raise upload timeout)
RETRIES = 3

# HEAD is main's 45; the bottom is your 60.
# Decide, delete the markers, then:
$ git add config.py
$ git rebase --continue
sections.tip: Prevention beats cure: small PRs, short-lived branches and syncing with main often keep each conflict small.
sections.pitfall: Committing a file that still contains `<<<<<<<` markers. Search for them before you `git add`, and run the tests; some teams have CI reject conflict markers.

activity.title: Resolve a real conflict
activity.prompt: Follow the steps until git stops with a conflict. Read both sides between the markers and decide what the final content should be, which may combine both. Remove every marker line, then stage the file and finish the merge. Notice that git only needs your help on the lines both branches changed.

check.question: During `git rebase origin/main`, a conflict shows `<<<<<<< HEAD`. Whose version is in the HEAD part?
choices: Your commit that is being replayed
The common ancestor of both branches
main's version, plus any of your commits already replayed
Whatever you last pushed to your remote branch
check.explanation: Rebase checks out main and re-applies your commits on top, so HEAD is the upstream side. Your commit being applied is the bottom part, labeled with its hash and message. In a plain merge it is the other way round.

sections.title: .gitignore and keeping secrets out
sections.key: Ignore what can be regenerated or is secret, commit lock files, and treat any secret that was ever pushed as leaked: rotate it, because history keeps it.
sections.body:
Your first `git status` lists 4,000 files in `node_modules/` and a `.env` holding the database password. A `.gitignore` tells git which untracked files to leave alone.

[[visual]]

Pattern rules: a trailing `/` matches only directories; a leading `/` anchors to the .gitignore's folder (`/build` skips `docs/build`); `*` matches anything but a slash; `!` re-includes what an earlier pattern excluded.

Two traps catch nearly everyone:

- `.gitignore` only affects **untracked** files. If `.env` was committed first, git keeps tracking it. `git rm --cached .env` stops that but keeps your copy.
- Deleting a committed secret does **not** remove it from history. **Rotate it** (revoke and replace) now, and tell your lead.

[[code]]

visual.title: What goes in .gitignore
rows: `package-lock.json`, `poetry.lock`: commit them so everyone installs the same versions

sections.code:
$ cat .gitignore
node_modules/
.venv/
__pycache__/
dist/
/build
.env
*.log
!keep-this.log

$ git rm --cached .env
rm '.env'
$ git commit -m "Stop tracking .env"
sections.deeper:
The usual pattern for configuration: commit a `.env.example` listing every variable with a dummy value, and ignore the real `.env`.

Rewriting history with a tool such as `git filter-repo` can remove a leaked secret from the repository, but it is a cleanup step, never a substitute for rotating: forks, clones and caches may already hold the old commits.

GitHub publishes starting templates for most languages in its `github/gitignore` repository.
sections.pitfall: Adding `.env` to `.gitignore` and assuming the leak is fixed. If it was ever pushed, the secret is in the history: rotate it.

check.question: `.env` is listed in .gitignore, but `git status` still shows it as modified. Why?
choices: The .gitignore file must be pushed before it takes effect
Patterns that start with a dot are not supported
.gitignore only applies to directories
The file was committed before the rule existed, and ignore rules skip tracked files
check.explanation: Ignore rules only stop untracked files from being added. A file that is already tracked stays tracked until you run git rm --cached on it and commit.

sections.title: Protected branches, CI, versions and tags
sections.key: Branch protection forces every change through a reviewed, green pull request; releases get SemVer numbers and annotated tags, which you must push explicitly.
sections.body:
On day one, `git push origin main` is rejected. That is **branch protection** at work:

[[visual]]

**Continuous integration** (CI), such as GitHub Actions, runs the checks on every push and PR, configured by a YAML file in `.github/workflows/`. When CI goes red, read the failing step's log, reproduce it locally and fix it in a new commit.

[[code]]

[[visual 2]]

A **tag** pins a name to a commit: `git tag -a v1.5.0 -m "Release 1.5.0"` makes an annotated tag. `git push` does **not** send tags: run `git push origin v1.5.0`, or `git push --tags`.

visual.title: Typical rules for main
rows: At least one reviewer, or a code owner for sensitive folders
Tests, linter and build must be green
The checks ran against the code that will land
History on main cannot be rewritten

visual.title: Semantic versioning, starting at 1.4.2
rows: Breaking change, such as removing a function (MAJOR)
First beta of the next major
visual.caption: npm ranges follow it: `^1.4.0` accepts any 1.x.y from 1.4.0 up, never 2.0.0; `~1.4.0` accepts only 1.4.x.

sections.code:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:     # the required check
  push:
    branches: [main]
    tags: ["v*"]     # release tags too
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: pytest
sections.deeper:
A plain `git tag v1.5.0` creates a lightweight tag, just a name; an annotated tag (`-a`) also stores the tagger, date and message, which is what releases should use. `git tag` lists tags, and `git switch --detach v1.5.0` lets you look at the released code.

Versions below 1.0.0 signal initial development, where anything may change. Pushing a tag often triggers a release workflow that builds and publishes the new version.

Never ask someone to bypass a required check because you are in a hurry: the check exists for exactly that moment.
sections.pitfall: Tagging a release and forgetting to push the tag. `git push` alone never sends tags, so the release workflow never runs and teammates cannot see it.

check.question: Your library removes a deprecated function that some users still call. The current version is 3.7.2. What is the next version under SemVer?
check.explanation: Removing something callers depend on is a breaking change, so MAJOR goes up and MINOR and PATCH reset: 4.0.0. A minor bump would tell users the upgrade is safe when it is not.

keyTerms.definition: A short-lived branch for one piece of work, merged into main through a pull request.
A proposal to merge a branch, where CI runs and teammates review the diff. GitLab calls it a merge request.
The remote branch your local branch tracks, set with git push -u, so push and pull need no arguments.
Merging a PR as one new commit on main that contains all of its changes.
Replaying your commits on top of another commit, creating new commits with new hashes and a linear history.
A safer force-push that refuses to overwrite the remote branch if it changed since your last fetch.
Two branches changed the same lines, so git marks both versions in the file and asks a human to decide.
Rules on a branch such as main: require PRs, approvals and passing checks, and block force pushes.
A CI job result reported on a pull request; required checks must pass before merging.
MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH numbering: breaking changes, backward-compatible features, bug fixes.
A tag that stores the tagger, date and message, created with git tag -a, used to mark releases.

summary: Branch from fresh main, push with `-u`, open a PR, merge when approved and green.
Imperative subjects, bodies that explain why, small PRs that say how to test.
Review the code, not the person; label severity and reply to every comment.
Merge keeps all, squash makes one commit, rebase makes a line; never rebase shared commits.
In a rebase conflict HEAD is main; resolve, test, add, then continue or abort.
Ignore dependencies, builds and secrets; rotate leaks; push release tags explicitly.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a new intern how a change travels from a ticket to a tagged release on your team: branches, pull requests, review, CI, merging and versioning, and what to do when a conflict appears on the way.

questions.question: You are on an up-to-date main. Create a branch named `feature/csv-export` and switch to it, in one command.
questions.explanation: git switch -c creates the branch at the current commit and moves onto it. git branch feature/csv-export would create it but leave you on main.

questions.question: Push your new local branch `feature/csv-export` to origin for the first time, setting it as the upstream so a plain `git push` works afterwards.
questions.explanation: -u is short for --set-upstream. It creates the remote branch and links your local branch to it, so later pushes and pulls need no arguments.

questions.question: Put the GitHub flow steps for one ticket in order.
items: Switch to main and pull the latest changes
Commit your changes in small steps
Push the branch and open a pull request
Address review comments and wait for CI to pass
Merge the pull request and delete the branch
questions.explanation: Start from fresh main, isolate the work on a branch, then let review and CI gate the merge. Deleting the merged branch keeps the branch list meaningful.

questions.question: Why do most teams keep feature branches short-lived?
choices: Git deletes branches automatically after 30 days
The longer a branch lives, the further main drifts and the bigger and riskier the merge
Long-lived branches slow down git status for everyone
Pull requests can contain at most 10 commits
questions.explanation: Every day a branch stays open, other changes land in main, so conflicts grow and the final merge carries more risk. Small, frequent merges keep each integration easy.

questions.question: You meant to branch from main but created `feature/b` while on `feature/a`, which is still in review. Your PR into main now shows 14 commits instead of your 3. Why?
choices: Your branch started from feature/a, so the PR includes feature/a's commits too
GitHub counts every commit pushed since your last pull
Git duplicates commits when you push twice
Merge commits are counted once per parent
questions.explanation: A PR shows every commit on your branch that main does not have. Because feature/b grew out of feature/a, its unmerged commits come along. Rebase your 3 commits onto main, or recreate the branch from main.

questions.question: Which of these are good commit message habits?
choices: An imperative subject such as "Add retry to file upload"
A subject of about 50 characters with no trailing period
A body that explains why the change was needed
Listing every changed file in the subject line
One logical change per commit
questions.explanation: The diff already lists the files. The message should summarize the change in the imperative and explain the reason, and each commit should be one coherent change that can be reviewed or reverted on its own.

questions.question: Match each Conventional Commits prefix to the change it describes.

pairs.right: Add an export button to the reports page
Stop the export crashing on empty reports
Split export.py into reader and writer modules, same behavior
Explain the export options in the README
Add missing tests for CSV escaping

questions.explanation: feat is a new capability, fix repairs a bug, refactor restructures without changing behavior, docs touches only documentation and test only adds or changes tests. Tools read these prefixes to build changelogs and choose version bumps.

questions.question: In a GitHub pull request description, which keyword before `#123` makes GitHub close issue 123 when the PR is merged? Type one keyword.
questions.explanation: GitHub recognizes close, fix and resolve in their various forms. The issue closes when the PR merges into the default branch, which keeps the tracker in sync without manual work.

questions.question: Your change touches 2,100 lines: a refactor of the data layer plus the new feature that needed it. What is the best way to get it reviewed?
choices: Open one PR and ask for a quick approval
Push it straight to main because it passed locally
Split it: a refactor-only PR first, then the feature in one or more smaller PRs
Open one PR and ask reviewers to skip the refactor files
questions.explanation: Small PRs get careful reviews and are easy to revert. A behavior-preserving refactor reviewed on its own is quick to check, and the feature PR on top of it becomes small and focused.

questions.question: Which of these review comments follow good etiquette?
choices: "What happens here if the list is empty?"
"nit: tmp could be pending_orders. Not blocking."
"Why would anyone write it this way?"
"This duplicates parse_date in utils/dates.py. Could we reuse that?"
"Wrong."
questions.explanation: Good comments ask questions, label how much they matter, and point to a concrete better option. Comments that judge the author or give no reason create defensiveness without helping anyone fix the code.

questions.question: A reviewer leaves 6 comments. You agree with 4 and think 2 are mistaken. What should you do?
choices: Fix the 4 and resolve all 6 threads without replying
Fix all 6 so the PR merges faster, even the ones you disagree with
Close the PR and open a new one without those comments
Fix the 4, and reply to the other 2 with your reasoning, open to discussion
questions.explanation: Every comment deserves a response. Explaining your reasoning either convinces the reviewer or surfaces something you missed. Silently resolving threads or blindly accepting changes both skip the conversation that makes review useful.

questions.question: What should you do just before you request a review?
choices: Squash every commit into one
Review your own diff as if you were the reviewer
Add every teammate as a reviewer
Mark every file as viewed
questions.explanation: A self-review catches leftover debug prints, commented-out code and missing tests, so your reviewer's time goes to the real questions.

questions.question: Why do reviewers label comments with prefixes such as `nit:`, `question:` or `blocking:`?
questions.answer: So the author knows how much each comment matters: a nit is optional polish, a question asks for an explanation, and blocking marks something that must change before merge. That keeps style preferences from holding up a PR and keeps real problems from being ignored.
questions.explanation: Without labels every comment looks equally urgent, and authors either fight over trivia or miss the one comment that mattered.

questions.question: Halfway through review you rewrite your branch with an interactive rebase and force-push. The reviewer is unhappy. What is the main reason?
choices: The old commits were replaced, so they can no longer see just what changed since their last review
Force-pushing deletes all comments on the pull request
GitHub refuses to merge a PR that was ever force-pushed
Rebasing automatically cancels all CI runs
questions.explanation: With new commits on top, the reviewer can look at only the new commits. A rewritten history forces them to re-read everything. Comments survive (on changed lines they are marked outdated). Tidy up with a rebase before review, or squash when merging.

questions.question: Match each merge button option to what it leaves on main.

pairs.right: Every branch commit plus a new commit with two parents
One new commit containing the whole pull request
Copies of each branch commit in a straight line, no merge commit

questions.explanation: Merge commits keep the full shape of history, squash keeps one commit per PR, and rebase keeps each commit but makes history linear.

questions.question: Your team squash-merges. After your PR merges, you keep committing on the same branch and open a second PR. It shows your old commits again and conflicts with main. Why?
choices: Squash merges are reverted automatically after a day
The squash made a new commit, so git does not see your original commits as merged; start a new branch from main
GitHub only allows one pull request per branch name
Your original commits were deleted from your local branch
questions.explanation: Squash merging copies the combined changes into a brand-new commit. Your branch's original commits are not ancestors of main, so git thinks they are still unmerged. Delete the branch after a squash merge and start fresh from main.

questions.question: Which of these breaks the golden rule of rebasing?
choices: Rebasing your own feature branch onto the latest main before review
Running git rebase -i to squash local commits you have not pushed
Rebasing your pushed PR branch that only you commit to, then pushing with --force-with-lease
Rebasing main onto your feature branch and force-pushing main
questions.explanation: main is shared: everyone has its commits and builds on them. Rewriting it leaves every teammate with history that no longer exists upstream. Rewriting your own branch is fine, as long as nobody else builds on it.

questions.question: You rebased your already-pushed feature branch, which tracks its remote. Update the remote branch, but refuse if someone else pushed to it since you last fetched.
questions.explanation: A rebased branch has new commits, so a normal push is rejected. --force-with-lease overwrites only if the remote still points where you last saw it, so a teammate's new commit is never silently destroyed. Plain --force skips that check.

questions.question: Before requesting review, you want to squash, reorder and reword the commits you made since branching from `main`. Type the command that opens that list.
questions.explanation: Interactive rebase lists every commit after main in an editor, where you mark each one pick, squash, fixup, reword or drop. Do it before others build on the commits.

questions.question: A rebase stopped on conflicts. Put the steps to finish it in order.
items: Run git status to see which files conflict
Edit each file to the correct final code
Stage the resolved files with git add
questions.explanation: Find the conflicts, decide the right code, remove every marker, prove it still works, then stage and tell git to continue replaying the remaining commits.

questions.question: A rebase stopped on a conflict. You fixed the file and staged it. Type the command that carries on with the rebase.
questions.explanation: --continue commits the resolved change and replays the next commit. Running git commit yourself in the middle of a rebase is a common mistake that makes the history messier.

questions.question: You started `git rebase origin/main`, hit conflicts in 12 files, and want to stop and put your branch back exactly as it was. Type the command.
questions.explanation: --abort ends the rebase and restores the branch to where it pointed before you started. Then you can try merging instead, or rebase in smaller steps.

questions.question: You see this while running `git rebase origin/main` on your feature branch. Which value came from your own commit?
questions.code:
<<<<<<< HEAD
MAX_UPLOAD_MB = 25
=======
MAX_UPLOAD_MB = 50
>>>>>>> 3f9c2a1 (Allow larger uploads for video)
choices: 25, because HEAD is always your branch
50, because during a rebase the bottom part is the commit being replayed
Neither: both values come from main's history
25, because the top part is always the newer change
questions.explanation: Rebase stands on main and re-applies your commits, so HEAD is main's version and the bottom part, labeled with your commit hash and message, is yours. In a plain merge the labels are the other way round.
questions.concept: ours and theirs in a rebase

questions.question: Right after a teammate merged main into their branch, CI fails with a SyntaxError in this file. What happened?
questions.code:
def upload_limit_mb(user):
<<<<<<< HEAD
    return 25 if user.is_free else 100
=======
    return 50 if user.is_free else 100
>>>>>>> main
choices: Python does not allow two return statements in one function
The merge used the wrong strategy and must be redone as a rebase
The function needs a docstring before its first statement
The conflict was committed unresolved; pick the right line and delete the marker lines
questions.explanation: The marker lines are not Python, so the file no longer parses. Resolve the block to one correct return, delete all three markers, run the tests, then commit. Searching for <<<<<<< before staging prevents this.

questions.question: You committed `.env` by mistake. Stop git tracking it, but keep the file on your disk.
questions.explanation: --cached removes the file from the index only, so the next commit deletes it from the repository while your local copy stays. Add .env to .gitignore so it is not re-added, and rotate any secrets it held if it was pushed.

questions.question: Which of these belong in a typical Node or Python project's .gitignore?
choices: node_modules/
.env
package-lock.json
__pycache__/
dist/
README.md
questions.explanation: Dependencies, secrets, caches and build output can be regenerated or must stay private. The lock file must be committed so everyone installs identical versions, and the README is documentation everyone needs.

questions.question: A teammate pushed an API key to main an hour ago, then deleted it in a new commit. What is the most important next step?
choices: Nothing: the deleting commit removed it
Add the key's file name to .gitignore
Revoke and replace the key now, because it is still in the repository history
Squash the two commits together locally
questions.explanation: Every clone and fork still contains the commit with the key, and bots scan public repositories for keys within minutes. Revoke it and issue a new one first; history cleanup comes after, if at all.

questions.question: In .gitignore, which single character at the start of a pattern re-includes a file that an earlier pattern excluded?
questions.explanation: A pattern like !keep-this.log negates an earlier *.log rule for that file. It cannot re-include a file whose parent directory is itself excluded.

questions.question: The current version is 1.4.2. Match each change to the next SemVer version.

pairs.left: Fix a crash when the input file is empty
First beta of the next major release

questions.explanation: Bug fixes bump PATCH, backward-compatible features bump MINOR, and anything that can break existing users bumps MAJOR. A hyphen suffix marks a pre-release that sorts before the final 2.0.0.

questions.question: You created the annotated tag `v1.5.0` locally. Push just that tag to origin.
questions.explanation: A plain git push sends branches, not tags. Name the tag explicitly, or use git push --tags to push every local tag.

questions.question: Which of these are typical branch protection rules for main?
choices: Require a pull request before merging
Require status checks to pass before merging
Require at least one approving review
Allow direct pushes from anyone whose last build was green
Block force pushes
questions.explanation: Protection exists so every change to main goes through review and green CI, and so its history cannot be rewritten. Allowing direct pushes would bypass both.

questions.question: package.json lists `"express": "^4.18.2"`. Which of these versions could npm install?
questions.explanation: A caret range accepts anything from 4.18.2 up to, but not including, the next major version 5.0.0. 4.17.9 is below the floor, and 5.0.0 might contain breaking changes.
